edits.old: - **Camera AEB is also headlight-limited.** IIHS night pedestrian-AEB ratings fell from superior to advanced with high beams, and to basic with low beams (§E6). Superior, advanced and basic are IIHS rating grades, in descending order.
edits.new: - **Camera AEB is also headlight-limited.** In IIHS research track tests of eight small SUVs (model years 2019–2022), each run in full darkness once with high beams and once with low beams and scored with IIHS's daylight pedestrian-AEB rating system, performance generally fell from superior to advanced with high beams and from superior to basic with low beams; only the radar-only Volkswagen Taos scored about as well as in daylight, and it was also the worst daytime performer [I, IIHS, 3 Feb 2022]. Superior, advanced and basic are IIHS rating grades, in descending order.
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-01.

edits.old: - The cited small IIHS track sample did not establish that better-rated headlights alone predict better night AEB results.
edits.new: - In that eight-vehicle sample, better-rated headlights did not go with better night scores: the two worst low-beam performers, the Honda CR-V and Volvo XC40, had good-rated headlights, and the Toyota C-HR outperformed all the others on low beams even with poor-rated headlights [I, IIHS, 3 Feb 2022].

edits.new: - IIHS measured the factory aim of both headlamps on 21 new 2015-model vehicles (three of each of seven models) and found aims between about 0.5° below and 0.4° above the horizontal, most of them below it [I].

edits.old: - It requires a 1° transition zone, against about 4° elsewhere.
edits.new: - Its transition zone, the part of the adaptive beam between a dimmed area and full high beam, may be no wider than 1° horizontally or vertically, and full high-beam photometry applies beyond it (FMVSS 108 S9.4.1.6.4.5) [P]. UN R48, UN R123 and SAE J3069 set no width for this zone; petitioners asked NHTSA for 4°, and Valeo and Koito showed ADB beams that need about 4° to reach full intensity. At 50 m a 1° zone is about 0.9 m wide and a 4° zone about 3.5 m ($50\times\tan1^\circ\approx0.87$ m; $50\times\tan4^\circ\approx3.50$ m), enough to cover an adjacent lane, which is why NHTSA kept 1° [P, NHTSA, 30 Dec 2024].
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-04.

edits.old: ADB also needs a camera to detect lamps at hundreds of metres, with some latency and transition zones.
edits.new: ADB also needs a camera to detect lamps at hundreds of metres, with some latency, and each shadow is bordered by transition zones that are not lit to full high-beam level (§A6.3).
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-04.

edits.old: - **Cruise (GM's robotaxi subsidiary), 2023:** its system discarded correct lidar data (Cummings).
edits.new: - **Cruise (GM's robotaxi subsidiary), 23 Mar 2023:** a driverless Cruise car ran into the back of an articulated San Francisco Muni bus that had pulled out of a stop ahead of it and then slowed. The software predicted the bus's motion from its front section, which the rear section had hidden, concluded that the bus was still moving and braked too late; Cruise recalled the software of 300 vehicles [P, Cruise recall report 23E-029]. Cummings reports that "the model rejected the lidar data that correctly detected the bus" [T, Cummings, *IEEE Spectrum*, 30 Jul 2023].
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-05.

edits.old: - With a 10% longitudinal tolerance, i.e. when a detection may be off in range (along the line of sight) by up to 10% of the distance, the camera's AP rises to about the lidar's: **camera error is almost purely depth**, and it grows with range [I]. The camera finds the objects; it misjudges how far away they are.
edits.new: - With a 10% longitudinal tolerance, i.e. when a detection may be off in range (along the line of sight) by up to 10% of the distance, the camera's vehicle AP (LET-3D-AP) rises to 89.7 at 0–30 m and 80.6 at 30–50 m, level with or slightly above the lidar's 88.5 and 78.5 under the same tolerance, and to 82.9 against 80.7 over all ranges [I]. Within 50 m, then, **camera error is almost purely depth**: the camera finds the objects but misjudges how far away they are. Beyond 50 m the tolerance lifts the camera only from 20.5 to 50.1, against the lidar's 66.2 (58.4 without tolerance), so at long range the camera also misses objects or places them off by more than 10% of their range [I].
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-06.

edits.old: Waymo's system was modified along the way (the recalls listed in §E1). Nor do they establish safety across all operating domains.
edits.new: Waymo's system was modified along the way (the recalls listed in §E1). Nor do they establish safety across all operating domains. No fatal crash in those miles has been attributed to the Waymo Driver [T, police statements relayed by NBC Bay Area and azfamily.com]: of the two fatal crashes Waymo reported to NHTSA before Jul 2026, one in San Francisco on 19 Jan 2025 began when a speeding car hit traffic queued behind a stopped, unoccupied Waymo, and in the other, in Tempe on 14 Sep 2025, a motorcyclist hit the back of a Waymo that was slowing to yield to a pedestrian and was then struck by a hit-and-run car [P, NHTSA Standing General Order reports]. A third, in Dallas on 7 Aug 2026, falls after these miles [P].
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-07.

edits.old: That is of the same order as the ≈110,000–120,000 points per frame that the dataset's own lidar records, whose grid is not given here; directions with no return, such as the sky, also lower a lidar's point count [E].
edits.new: That is of the same order as the 116,096 points per frame, on average (74,386–133,538), that the dataset's own lidar records [P, Zhang et al., *Sci. Data* 2025, Table 4]. That lidar is a RoboSense RS-Ruby Lite, with 80 channels spread non-uniformly over a 40° vertical field (−25° to +15°) and 0.2° azimuth steps at the dataset's 10 Hz frame rate, so its own grid has $(360/0.2)\times80=1{,}800\times80=144{,}000$ angular cells per frame, matching its rated 1.44 M points per second at 10 Hz [P, RoboSense manual]. The average frame fills about 81% of those cells ($116{,}096/144{,}000\approx0.81$), because directions with no return, such as the sky, lower a lidar's point count [E].
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-08.

edits.new: Magna's thermal camera is roughly the size of a golf ball; its fifth generation was targeted to debut in late 2025, and Magna aims eventually at sugar-cube size [P, Magna, May 2024].

edits.new: Chinese makers such as Raytron and Guide (Wuhan Guide Infrared) offer cheaper sensors and optics [U], and pixel pitch has fallen to 8 µm and below: Raytron released an 8 µm 1920×1080 detector in 2021 and a 6 µm 640×512 detector in 2024, and Guide shows an 8 µm 640×512 camera core [P].

edits.old: - Thermal is therefore valuable on unlit rural roads and highways, where many night pedestrian deaths occur.
edits.new: - Thermal is therefore most valuable where roads are unlit at night. In 2024, 2,376 of the 7,080 US pedestrian deaths (34%) happened in the dark on roads without lighting; 70% of these were in urban areas and 29% in rural areas, and by road type 56% were on arterials other than freeways, 22% on interstates and freeways and 21% on collectors and local roads [I, NHTSA FARS 2024; E].
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-10.

edits.old: - Chinese thermal makers buy optics domestically; Western ones face permit friction, because China requires export permits for germanium.
edits.new: - China has required export licences for germanium since August 2023 and banned germanium exports to the United States in December 2024 [I, USGS MCS 2026]; the US ban is suspended from 9 Nov 2025 to 27 Nov 2026 [T, Pillsbury, Nov 2025]. A thermal-camera maker outside China that buys Chinese germanium or lenses therefore depends on licensed shipments, whereas a Chinese maker buying at home does not [E].

edits.old: - Just below the cutoff sits the "hotspot", the brightest part of the beam, typically tens of thousands of cd.
edits.new: - Just below the cutoff sits the "hotspot", the brightest part of the beam, typically tens of thousands of cd: UN R149 requires a class B passing beam to deliver at least 10,100 cd at points 50R and 75R, just below the cutoff on the kerb side (Table 8), and puts the maximum of an adaptive class C passing beam between 16,900 and 44,100 cd (Table 9) [P].

edits.new: - **Europe and China:** on sale since late 2013, when Audi's Matrix LED headlights, with 25 individually switched high-beam LEDs per lamp, arrived on the A8 [P, Audi, Jul 2013]; Mercedes followed with Multibeam LED on the CLS in 2014 [T], and Mercedes Digital Light, BMW Selective Beam and many Chinese makers' systems came later.

edits.new: Example: at the ECE glare point B50L a conventional class A or B passing beam may send at most 350 cd, with no minimum (UN R112 §6.2.4; UN R149 Table 8), and the class C passing beam of an adaptive front-lighting system (AFS) must stay within 50–350 cd (UN R149 Table 9) [P].

edits.old: - Chalcogenide glass (infrared-transmitting glass based on sulphur, selenium or tellurium; e.g. LightPath "BlackDiamond", Ge-free) is **one demonstrated substitute** in infrared optics, not a universal replacement for every thermal-camera lens design [I, USGS].
edits.new: - Chalcogenide glass (infrared-transmitting glass based on sulphur, selenium or tellurium) is **one demonstrated substitute** in infrared optics, not a universal replacement for every thermal-camera lens design [I, USGS]. Not every chalcogenide glass is germanium-free: LightPath's BlackDiamond BD6 is an arsenic selenide ($\mathrm{As_{40}Se_{60}}$) with no germanium, whereas its BD-2 grade is 28% germanium [P, LightPath datasheets].
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-12.

edits.old: IIHS (the US Insurance Institute for Highway Safety) scores visibility as the distance at which 5 lux reaches a point 25 cm above the lane edge; 3 lux is a common criterion for low-contrast objects [P, IIHS].
edits.new: IIHS (the US Insurance Institute for Highway Safety) scores visibility, for low and high beams alike, as the distance at which 5 lux reaches a point 25 cm above the lane edge. Its rationale calls 3 lux probably the most common single criterion for the visibility of low-contrast objects, and chose 5 lux because it can be measured more accurately in moving tests and tracks the 3 lux distance [P, IIHS].
edits.why: Source found by the R1_partA_E2-E5 research agent; see sources/R1_partA_E2-E5_findings.md, R1_partA_E2-E5-13.

edits.new: - Measurement agrees: in a closed-road study, drivers using low beams against oncoming glare recognized only 5% of black-clad pedestrians (Wood, Tyrrell & Carberry 2005) [I], against about 40% without glare [U].

edits.new: - **Measured:** switching from low to high beam raised mean pedestrian recognition distance from 59 m to 94 m, and by up to 3.5× for dark clothing (Wood, Tyrrell & Carberry 2003 and 2005) [U].
